prompt: The telephone network reserved a circuit for each call. What did the internet put in its place?
hint: Think about what has to happen if nothing is held open for you.

choices.text: Nothing is reserved, and each piece carries its own destination
choices.why: With no path held open, the addressing has to travel with the data.

choices.text: A slower kind of circuit, reserved for a handful of callers at a time
choices.why: There is no circuit at all, shared or otherwise.

choices.text: A circuit that is reserved for you, but released whenever you go quiet
choices.why: That is still a reservation, and nothing reserves anything here.

choices.text: A single path chosen once and kept for the whole transfer
choices.why: Two packets of one message may take different paths, seconds apart.

prompt: A router receives a packet carrying part of an encrypted video call. What does it read?
hint: Ask what it needs in order to do its one job.

choices.text: It reads no field, and repeats the packet out of its other ports
choices.why: It reads the destination; forwarding blindly is what a hub did, and hubs are gone.

choices.text: The payload, to check the call is permitted
choices.why: Reading payloads is exactly what the design avoids — it is why encryption works.

choices.text: The header, and mostly just the destination
choices.why: Where to send it next is the whole question a router answers.

choices.text: The whole packet, to decide how urgent it is
choices.why: It does not open the payload, so it cannot know what kind of data this is.

prompt: The pieces of one message travel independently. Which of these follow from that? Choose all that apply.
hint: Consider what nothing is coordinating on their behalf.

choices.text: They can arrive in a different order from the one they were sent in
choices.why: Different routes and different queues, so different arrival times.

choices.text: They are kept together so that they arrive as a group
choices.why: Nothing is escorting them — that is what 'independently' means.

choices.text: They can take different routes across the network
choices.why: Each machine decides for each packet on its own.

choices.text: They are re-ordered by the last router before delivery
choices.why: Nothing in the middle reassembles anything; that is the ends' job.

choices.text: One of them can be dropped without anybody reporting it
choices.why: Best effort means the network will not tell you it failed.

prompt: Fill the two blanks: a packet is made of a ___, which machines along the way read, and a ___, which they do not.
hint: One is the label, the other is the load.

prompt: Why is a packet header kept deliberately small?
hint: Think about how many times it is paid for.

choices.text: Encryption requires the header to stay under a size limit
choices.why: The header is not encrypted, and no such limit exists.

choices.text: Routers are built to read a fixed number of bytes and would ignore the rest
choices.why: There is no such limit; the constraint is cost, not capability.

choices.text: It rides on every packet, so its cost is multiplied by all traffic
choices.why: A page of two thousand packets pays for that label two thousand times.

choices.text: A larger header would no longer fit inside the frame that has to carry it
choices.why: Frames are far larger than any header; that is not the binding constraint.

prompt: A packet crosses four machines on its way to a server. How many frames carried it?
hint: Count the hops, not the machines.

choices.text: As many as there are switches along the way
choices.why: Switches do not build frames; routers do.

choices.text: One, wrapped when it was sent and unwrapped when it finally arrived
choices.why: That is the packet. A frame does not survive a router.

choices.text: Two — one for the local network and one for everything beyond it
choices.why: Every hop rebuilds it, not just the first and last.

choices.text: One per hop, each built and discarded at that hop
choices.why: A frame lives for exactly one step of the journey.

prompt: Match each box to what it does with a frame that arrives.
hint: One of them never finds out where the packet is ultimately going.

pairs.right: Sends the same frame out of a different port
Discards the frame and builds a new one for the next hop
Opens the frame and keeps what was inside

right_distractors: Rewrites the packet's destination before passing it on
Holds the frame until the whole message has arrived

prompt: Where does a frame stop?
hint: It ends where something has to read the packet inside.

choices.text: At the first switch, which is where one network ends and another begins
choices.why: A switch moves a frame between ports without opening it.

choices.text: At the first router
choices.why: A router opens it, reads the packet, and builds a new frame.

choices.text: Wherever the cable it is on physically ends
choices.why: A cable can end at a switch, which is not a stop for the frame.

choices.text: At the destination machine, like the packet
choices.why: That is the packet's journey. The frame ended many hops earlier.

prompt: Wi-Fi was invented and became the usual way people connect, without any packet header changing. Why was that possible? Choose all that apply.
hint: Think about what each of the two envelopes is responsible for.

choices.text: Packets were extended with a field saying which medium they crossed
choices.why: No such field exists, and needing one would defeat the separation.

choices.text: Each layer can change without the other being touched
choices.why: Which is the benefit that pays for having two envelopes instead of one.

choices.text: Wi-Fi frames are translated into Ethernet frames by the router in between
choices.why: They are not converted; the old frame is discarded and a new one is built.

choices.text: The packet's addressing is the same regardless of what carries it
choices.why: That is the whole point of separating the two.

choices.text: The frame is what the medium defines, and the medium is what changed
choices.why: Radio needed a different frame; the packet inside was unaffected.

prompt: A frame arrives with a checksum that does not match its contents. What happens?
hint: Ask who is told.

choices.text: It is discarded and the sender is asked to send it again
choices.why: No complaint is sent; the ends find out only by noticing nothing arrived.

choices.text: It is passed on, and the destination repairs it
choices.why: A corrupted frame is thrown away where the corruption is detected.

choices.text: The router repairs it from the checksum
choices.why: A checksum detects corruption; it does not carry enough to repair it.

choices.text: It is discarded, and nothing is sent back to say so
choices.why: To the two ends it is indistinguishable from a packet dropped in a queue.

prompt: Which machine on the path holds the route from your laptop to a server?
hint: Ask what each one is actually storing.

choices.text: Your laptop, which computes it before sending
choices.why: Your laptop knows its own network and one default gateway.

choices.text: The destination, which advertises the path back
choices.why: Nothing advertises paths to individual machines.

choices.text: None of them — each knows only the next step
choices.why: The path is an outcome of a dozen independent decisions, not a plan.

choices.text: The first router, which chooses the path for the whole journey
choices.why: It chooses one next hop, and has no say in what happens afterwards.

prompt: A routing table has a line for `203.0.113.0`–`203.0.113.255` and another for `203.0.0.0`–`203.255.255.255`. A packet arrives for `203.0.113.7`. Which line is used?
hint: Both of them match. Something has to break the tie.

choices.text: The one written first, because a table is read from the top downwards
choices.why: Order in the file does not decide it; specificity does.

choices.text: The narrower one, because the most specific match wins
choices.why: It covers 256 addresses against sixteen million, so it is the answer.

choices.text: The wider one, because it covers more addresses
choices.why: Covering more is exactly why it loses to a more specific line.

choices.text: Both of them, and a copy of the packet is sent down each of the two
choices.why: One packet takes one next hop.

prompt: Fill the blank: the last line of a routing table covers everything unfamiliar, and the neighbour it points at is called the default ___.
hint: It is a field in your own network settings.

prompt: Router A believes the way forward is B, and B believes it is A. What stops the packet bouncing for ever?
hint: Something in the packet is getting smaller at every step.

choices.text: The sender notices that no answer is coming back and gives up by itself
choices.why: The sender is told nothing, and the loop would continue regardless.

choices.text: The packet expires once a fixed number of seconds have passed since sending
choices.why: The field counts hops, despite being called time to live.

choices.text: The two routers notice they disagree and repair their tables between them
choices.why: Nothing here detects it — the defence is blunt on purpose.

choices.text: A counter in the header reaches zero and the packet is discarded
choices.why: Nobody detects the loop; the packet simply runs out of chances.

prompt: `traceroute` works by sending packets with the hop counter set to 1, then 2, then 3. Which of these follow from that? Choose all that apply.
hint: The output is assembled from many separate probes.

choices.text: It reveals the routers by making each one discard a packet in turn
choices.why: Each reply comes from the router that reduced the counter to zero.

choices.text: It asks the first router for its table and prints the route out of that
choices.why: No table is read; the route is inferred from replies.

choices.text: Different lines can describe different paths
choices.why: Nothing guarantees every probe took the same route.

choices.text: A hop can appear blank, because a router may decline to answer
choices.why: Sending that message back is optional, and many do not.

choices.text: It shows the path the earlier packets of your connection took
choices.why: It shows what these probes met, which is not a record of anything else.

prompt: An Ethernet link has an MTU of 1500 bytes, of which 20 are the packet header. How many bytes of your data fit in one packet?
hint: Take the header off the ceiling.

prompt: You send 4000 bytes of data over links with an MTU of 1500, where each packet spends 20 bytes on its header. How many packets does it take?
hint: Each packet carries at most 1480 bytes of your data, and a remainder still costs a whole packet.

prompt: A router cannot pass a packet marked *do not fragment* because it is too big. What does it do?
hint: There are only two options, and this one is not cutting it up.

choices.text: Passes it along unchanged and leaves the next link to work out what to do
choices.why: It cannot: the frame would not fit on the outgoing medium.

choices.text: Holds on to it until a link with more room happens to become available
choices.why: Routers do not hold packets waiting for the network to change.

choices.text: Cuts it into fragments regardless, on the grounds that delivery matters more
choices.why: The mark forbids exactly that.

choices.text: Discards it and sends a message back saying the largest size it takes
choices.why: The sender is then expected to try again with smaller packets.

prompt: Somebody on a VPN reports that logging in works and short pages load, but one large page hangs for ever. What does that pattern point at?
hint: Notice which requests succeed and which do not.

choices.text: The server being overloaded by whatever it takes to build the large page
choices.why: An overloaded server would be slow for small requests too.

choices.text: Oversized packets refused, with the warning being discarded on the way back
choices.why: The sender never learns, so it retransmits the same too-big packet.

choices.text: The name of that one address failing to resolve on this particular machine
choices.why: A name that does not resolve fails immediately and for everything on that host.

choices.text: The VPN quietly dropping the connection once some timeout has been reached
choices.why: Small requests on the same connection keep working, so it is not dropped.

prompt: Why is fragmenting a packet unattractive? Choose all that apply.
hint: Think about where the pieces are put back together.

choices.text: Reassembly happens only at the final destination
choices.why: No router in between puts it back together.

choices.text: Every fragment has its own chance of being lost
choices.why: Three fragments give three opportunities to fail instead of one.

choices.text: Losing one fragment wastes all of them
choices.why: Nothing can be reassembled until every piece has arrived.

choices.text: Fragments are always sent along different routes
choices.why: They may or may not be; nothing forces them apart.

choices.text: A fragmented packet loses its destination address
choices.why: Each fragment carries a header with the destination on it.

prompt: Fill the two blanks: an ___ gets the data to the right machine, and a ___ gets it to the right program on that machine.
hint: One is a building, the other is a door in it.

prompt: You open the same site in two tabs. Why do the two sets of answers not get mixed up?
hint: A connection is identified by more than the destination.

choices.text: Each tab is handed an address of its own by the operating system underneath
choices.why: Both tabs share the machine's one address.

choices.text: Each connection uses a different source port, so the four numbers differ
choices.why: Source address, source port, destination address and destination port.

choices.text: The server is careful to send the answers back in the order it was asked in
choices.why: Order would not tell the two apart, and nothing promises it.

choices.text: The browser tags each request with the tab it came from
choices.why: Nothing in the packet names a tab; the separation is by port.

prompt: You start a development server and are told the address is already in use. What happened?
hint: Listening is a claim, not a habit.

choices.text: The machine has run out of the port numbers it is allowed to hand out
choices.why: There are tens of thousands, and this message is about one of them.

choices.text: Another machine on the same network has already taken that port number
choices.why: Ports are claimed per machine; another machine's port 3000 is unrelated.

choices.text: Another program has already claimed that port on this machine
choices.why: Often a copy of the same program that was never stopped.

choices.text: That port is reserved by convention for a different service elsewhere
choices.why: A convention does not prevent a program binding; an existing claim does.

prompt: Where does a TCP connection actually exist?
hint: Ask what the routers in the middle are keeping.

choices.text: In the packets themselves, each of which names the connection it belongs to
choices.why: Nothing in a packet says which conversation it is part of.

choices.text: In the memory of the two machines at the ends, and nowhere else
choices.why: Both keep notes; the middle forwards on the destination alone.

choices.text: In the routers along the path, which track open connections
choices.why: Routers have no idea a connection exists.

choices.text: In the first router, which set it up on the sender's behalf
choices.why: Nothing sets a connection up on your behalf.

prompt: Match each port number to what usually listens on it.
hint: Two of them are the same service with and without encryption.

pairs.right: SSH, for getting into the machine itself

prompt: What does TCP convert loss into, and what does UDP convert it into?
hint: One of them waits, the other carries on.

choices.text: TCP turns loss into delay; UDP turns it into absence
choices.why: Which is the whole trade, stated in one line.

choices.text: Both turn loss into delay, at different speeds
choices.why: UDP never resends anything, so nothing is delayed by loss.

choices.text: Both turn loss into absence, but TCP reports it
choices.why: TCP recovers the data rather than reporting it missing.

choices.text: TCP turns loss into absence, and UDP is the one that turns it into delay
choices.why: That is the two swapped: it is TCP that resends and waits.

prompt: Packet 3 is lost. Packets 4 and 5 arrived intact. Why does TCP not hand 4 and 5 to the program?
hint: Consider the one guarantee TCP exists to make.

choices.text: Delivering them now would put the stream out of order
choices.why: This is head-of-line blocking: one gap holds up everything behind it.

choices.text: They are unreadable until the piece in front of them has been decrypted
choices.why: Ordering has nothing to do with encryption.

choices.text: They were discarded as soon as the gap left by 3 was noticed by the receiver
choices.why: They are held in memory, not thrown away.

choices.text: The program has not got round to asking for them yet, so they wait
choices.why: The program is waiting; what is missing is the piece in front.

prompt: Match each use to the transport that suits it, and to why.
hint: Ask whether the data is still worth having late.

pairs.right: TCP — every byte matters and nothing is urgent
UDP — audio that arrives late is useless audio
UDP — one small question, cheaper to ask again than to agree first

right_distractors: TCP — because the answer is too large for one packet
UDP — because the data is encrypted end to end

prompt: HTTP/3 is built on UDP. Which of these are reasons? Choose all that apply.
hint: It is not because reliability stopped mattering.

choices.text: UDP packets are given faster routes across the network than TCP ones are
choices.why: Routers do not treat them differently; they read the same destination.

choices.text: It rebuilds ordering and retransmission per stream instead
choices.why: So one stalled download no longer holds up the other nine.

choices.text: Over one TCP connection a single loss stalls every transfer sharing it
choices.why: Head-of-line blocking applied to the whole connection.

choices.text: UDP is a floor to build on when TCP is not quite the right shape
choices.why: A port and nothing else, which leaves room for something different.

choices.text: Reliability turned out not to matter much for fetching pages over the web
choices.why: A page missing a fragment is broken; HTTP/3 is entirely reliable.

prompt: Put TCP's response to a lost packet in order.
hint: Nothing happens until something does not happen.
items: The receiver acknowledges the packets that did arrive
No acknowledgement comes back for one of them in time
The sender transmits that data a second time
The receiver puts the stream back in order and hands it over
trap: The common swap is putting the retransmission before the missing acknowledgement — the sender has nothing to react to until an acknowledgement fails to arrive.

prompt: Put each name on the field it belongs to.
hint: Two of the four are addresses, and only one of them is where the packet is going.

prompt: Put the life of one packet in order, from the moment it is built.
hint: The frame is built later than you might expect, and rebuilt more often.
items: The message is cut into pieces and each is given a destination
A frame is built for the first cable and the packet goes inside it
A router discards that frame, reads the packet and builds a new one
The destination opens the last frame and keeps the packet
The port decides which program on that machine receives it
trap: The common swap is putting the port before the frames — the port is only consulted once the packet has arrived at the machine, long after every frame has done its work.

prompt: Match each thing to the distance it survives.
hint: Two of these are rebuilt more often than the others.

pairs.right: The whole journey, end to end
One hop, then it is discarded
Only in the memory of the two ends

right_distractors: Until the next router reassembles it
As long as the routing table is unchanged

prompt: A download is slow, and someone says the routers are prioritising other traffic over it. What is wrong with that explanation?
hint: Ask what a router can actually tell about your packets.

choices.text: A router does not open the payload, so it cannot tell what the traffic is
choices.why: It reads the destination and forwards; the application is invisible to it.

choices.text: It is the first router on the path, not the others, that can prioritise
choices.why: The problem is not which router; it is that the content is not visible.

choices.text: Routers do prioritise, but by source address rather than by what is inside
choices.why: The claim is not about which field — it is that content is not readable at all.

choices.text: Nothing is wrong with it — routers do inspect the contents of every packet
choices.why: Inspecting payloads is what the design deliberately avoids.

prompt: Fill the two blanks: a ___ moves a frame between ports without opening it, while a ___ discards the frame and builds a new one.
hint: One of them never sees the packet inside.

prompt: A link has an MTU of 1500 bytes. The packet header takes 20 and the TCP header takes another 20. How many bytes of your data fit in one packet?
hint: Two headers, not one.

prompt: Two requests are sent at the same instant and the second one answers first. What should you conclude?
hint: Ask what was ever promised about order.

choices.text: Nothing is wrong — no order was ever promised between them
choices.why: They are separate exchanges, and nothing coordinates their timing.

choices.text: The connection must have reordered the two of them somewhere on the path
choices.why: Reordering inside one stream is repaired by TCP; these are two streams.

choices.text: The first request was lost on the way and silently sent a second time
choices.why: A retransmission is invisible and would not make the second answer first.

choices.text: The server is processing the requests in the wrong sequence internally
choices.why: A server answering two requests is not obliged to finish them in order.

prompt: A connection hangs completely. Small requests to the same machine work. What is the most likely cause of the shapes you have met in this lesson?
hint: It is the failure caused by a message that was supposed to come back.

choices.text: Oversized packets refused, and the too-big warning discarded on the way back
choices.why: The sender never learns and retransmits the same packet for ever.

choices.text: The hop counter ran down to zero somewhere along the path and it was dropped
choices.why: That discards a packet; small requests would be affected equally.

choices.text: There is no program listening on the destination port of that machine
choices.why: That refuses instantly rather than hanging.

choices.text: No line of any routing table on the path covers that destination address
choices.why: That fails for everything to that machine, including small requests.

prompt: Which of these does a packet NOT carry? Choose all that apply.
hint: Four of the six are somebody else's job.

choices.text: The connection it belongs to
choices.why: A connection lives in the two ends' memory.

choices.text: The route it will take
choices.why: It carries a destination; each machine decides the next step alone.

choices.text: The address it is going to
choices.why: The destination is the field a router reads.

choices.text: A guarantee that it will arrive
choices.why: Best effort is the whole promise.

choices.text: How many bytes long it is
choices.why: Length is in the header.

choices.text: Its position in the message
choices.why: That belongs to TCP, above the packet.

prompt: Why does a UDP-based video call survive a lost packet better than a TCP-based file transfer would?
hint: Ask whether the missing piece is still worth having.

choices.text: Video and audio data is not really affected by a packet going missing
choices.why: It is affected — the point is that the gap costs less than the wait.

choices.text: UDP packets are smaller ones, so less of the call is lost when one goes
choices.why: Size is not what differs; what differs is what happens next.

choices.text: UDP notices the loss and retransmits it faster than TCP would have done
choices.why: UDP does not retransmit at all.

choices.text: The missing audio was due milliseconds ago, so carrying on beats waiting
choices.why: Delivering it now would be worse than the gap.

prompt: Put the three-way handshake in order, and then the first data.
hint: Nothing of what was actually being asked for travels until the third message.
items: The browser sends a SYN with the number it will start counting from
The server answers with a SYN-ACK, accepting and sending its own number
The browser sends the ACK, agreeing
trap: The common swap is putting the request before the ACK — it can ride along with it, but never before it, which is why the connection costs a full round trip before any work starts.

prompt: Fill the two blanks: a connection is identified by four numbers, and when two tabs talk to the same server the only one that differs is the ___ ___.
hint: It is the number your own machine picks for each new connection.
